Which statement is not correct?
questions.stemText: X-rays are produced when high speed electrons collide with a tungsten target as shown in the diagram below. The graph below illustrates variation of wavelength with intensity of X-rays. Which statement is not correct? A The cut-off wavelength corresponds to the least energetic photon released. B A continuous spectrum with a minimum wavelength is caused by the braking radiation. C X-ray photons are produced when the electrons in the outer shells transit to the inner shells. D The sharp characteristic peaks at well-defined wavelengths are caused by transitions of electrons between energy levels in the tungsten.

options.label: A
options.text: The cut-off wavelength corresponds to the least energetic photon released.

options.label: B
options.text: A continuous spectrum with a minimum wavelength is caused by the braking radiation.

options.label: C
options.text: X-ray photons are produced when the electrons in the outer shells transit to the inner shells.

options.label: D
options.text: The sharp characteristic peaks at well-defined wavelengths are caused by transitions of electrons between energy levels in the tungsten.

questions.difficultyReason: The false statement follows directly from the inverse energy–wavelength relation.
questions.misconception: Associating shorter wavelengths with lower photon energies

explanation.body: The cut-off wavelength is the shortest wavelength present. Since $E=hc/\lambda$, it corresponds to the most energetic photon released.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Braking radiation from decelerating electrons produces the continuous spectrum with a short-wavelength cutoff.
perOption.C: Outer-shell electrons can emit X-rays when they fill vacancies in inner shells.
perOption.D: The sharp peaks arise from transitions between discrete energy levels in tungsten.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Which statement about the Heisenberg position-momentum uncertainty principle on a particle is not correct?

A The exact values of momentum $p$ and position $x$ cannot be achieved simultaneously.
B The uncertainty of momentum $\Delta p$ is in the same direction as the uncertainty of position $\Delta x$.
C The product of uncertainties of momentum $\Delta p$ and position $\Delta x$ will always be greater than the Planck constant.
D The uncertainties of momentum $\Delta p$ and position $\Delta x$ can be minimised concurrently with the same experimental equipment.

stemImage.alt: Question 28: Which statement about the Heisenberg position-momentum uncertainty principle on a particle is not correct?

questions.difficultyReason: The student must distinguish the intrinsic trade-off from experimental limits and read the bound precisely.
questions.misconception: Treating quantum uncertainty as an equipment limitation

explanation.body: These uncertainties arise from the wave nature of matter and persist regardless of the equipment. Reducing the position spread raises the lower bound on the corresponding momentum spread, so equipment cannot make both spreads arbitrarily small together.

perOption.A: Exact position and its corresponding momentum component cannot be achieved simultaneously.
perOption.B: The uncertainty relation pairs position and momentum components along the same axis.
perOption.C: This statement is also false as written because the standard-deviation bound is $\Delta x\,\Delta p_x\ge h/(4\pi)$, allowing the product to be below $h$.
perOption.D: Correct.

It is illuminated with ultraviolet radiation and photoelectrons are emitted. The variation with the electromotive force (e.m.f.) supplied of the current is obtained.

Which graph will be obtained if the experiment is repeated with a higher intensity of the ultraviolet radiation of the same frequency?

[Graph of current against e.m.f. with zero marked on both axes. From highest to lowest saturation current, the curves are labelled A, B, original graph, C and D. A and D share the original graph’s negative e.m.f. intercept. B and C share an intercept farther to the left.]

questions.misconception: Confusing photon energy with photon arrival rate

explanation.body: Higher intensity at the same frequency delivers more photons per second, so more photoelectrons are emitted per second and the saturation current increases. Photon energy $hf$ and maximum photoelectron kinetic energy $hf-\phi$ stay the same, so the stopping potential is unchanged. Curve A shows both features.

X-rays are produced when electrons are accelerated from rest by a potential difference and collide with a metal target.

The minimum wavelength of X-rays produced is $\lambda_0$.

What is the minimum wavelength of X-rays produced if the momentum of the electrons when they collide with the metal target is doubled?

A $\lambda_0/4$
B $\lambda_0/2$
C $2\lambda_0$
D $4\lambda_0$

questions.misconception: Applying the electron de Broglie relation to the emitted X-ray

explanation.body: The highest-energy X-ray photon can receive the electron’s entire kinetic energy, so $hc/\lambda_{\min}=p^2/(2m_e)$ in the nonrelativistic model. Doubling $p$ quadruples that energy and gives a new minimum wavelength of $\lambda_0/4$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats maximum photon energy as proportional to the electron’s momentum, or uses the electron’s de Broglie wavelength.
perOption.C: Makes wavelength increase linearly with electron momentum.
perOption.D: Correctly obtains a fourfold increase in energy but makes wavelength increase with it.

questions.misconception: Assuming the work function changes the graph gradient

explanation.body: The photoelectric equation is $hf=\Phi+eV_s$, with $\Phi=hf_m$. Thus $V_s=(h/e)f-\Phi/e$. A smaller work function lowers the threshold frequency while the gradient remains $h/e$, so the line shifts left and stays parallel to the original.

questions.stemText:
A 3.1 mW beam of electromagnetic radiation comprising photons each with energy 3.11 eV is incident on a clean metal plate M. The potential difference $V$ is varied until the ammeter gives a maximum reading of $2.0\ \mu\mathrm{A}$.

[Electromagnetic radiation strikes plate M, the left plate in a two-electrode tube. The electrodes are connected in series with an ammeter A and a variable voltage source $V$.]

What is the ratio (electrons emitted per unit time) / (photons incident per unit time)?

A $3.2\times10^{-22}$
B $2.0\times10^{-3}$
C 1.0
D $1.3\times10^{16}$

stemImage.alt: Question 27: A 3.1 mW beam of electromagnetic radiation comprising photons each with energy 3.11 eV is incident on a clean metal plate M. The potential difference V is varie

questions.difficultyReason: The student must calculate two particle rates and convert photon energy to joules.
questions.misconception: Using current directly as a particle rate

explanation.body: The electron emission rate at maximum current is $I/e=(2.0\times10^{-6})/(1.6\times10^{-19})=1.25\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The incident photon rate is $P/E_\gamma=(3.1\times10^{-3})/(3.11\times1.6\times10^{-19})=6.23\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The ratio is $(1.25\times10^{13})/(6.23\times10^{15})=2.0\times10^{-3}$.

perOption.A: This uses the current directly without converting it to electrons per second.
perOption.B: Correct. About two electrons are emitted per thousand incident photons.
perOption.C: This assumes that every incident photon ejects an electron.
perOption.D: This omits the electronvolt-to-joule conversion for the photon rate.

In the lungs, there are tiny sacs of air known as alveoli. The average diameter of an alveolus is 0.250 mm. Consider an oxygen molecule of mass $5.30\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg}$ that is trapped in an alveolus. What is the order of magnitude of the uncertainty in the velocity of this oxygen molecule?

A $10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
B $10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
C $10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
D $10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

questions.difficultyReason: The student must convert position confinement to a momentum and then velocity uncertainty scale.
questions.misconception: Leaving the confinement length in millimetres

explanation.body: Use the syllabus estimate $\Delta p_x\Delta x\gtrsim h$, with $\Delta p_x=m\Delta v$ and $\Delta x=0.25\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$. Substitution gives $(5.30\times10^{-26}\Delta v)(0.25\times10^{-3})\gtrsim6.63\times10^{-34}$. The closest offered velocity uncertainty scale is $10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. This is the closest offered uncertainty scale.
perOption.B: Using the diameter in millimetres as though it were in metres lowers the estimate by a factor of a thousand.
perOption.C: This assigns too little momentum spread for confinement to an alveolus.
perOption.D: This would require a much larger confinement length for a molecule of the given mass.

[Four columns of horizontal energy levels are labelled A, B, C and D from left to right, with their ground levels aligned. A dashed horizontal line is drawn at energy $W$ above the ground state. A has one excited level above $W$ and one below it. B has one above $W$, one just below it and one lower excited level. C has four excited levels below $W$, the highest slightly below B’s highest reachable level. D has four excited levels below $W$, the highest below the highest reachable levels of A, B and C.]

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding the largest accessible energy drop and relating it to photon wavelength.
questions.misconception: Using an excited level above the incident electron energy.

explanation.body: The shortest wavelength corresponds to the highest photon frequency, and the photon energy $hf$ equals the energy difference between the levels. For each atom, the largest possible drop is from the highest level reachable with energy $W$ down to the ground state. Atom B has the largest such energy difference.

perOption.A: A’s level above $W$ cannot be reached, and its accessible excited level gives a smaller drop than B’s.

questions.stemText:
$\lambda_0$ is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of $1\ \mathrm{kV}$.

$\lambda_1$ is the de Broglie wavelength of another electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of $100\ \mathrm{kV}$.

What is the value of the ratio $\frac{\lambda_0}{\lambda_1}$?

A 0.1
B 1
C 10
D 100

stemImage.alt: Question 28: λ0 is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 1 kV. λ 1 is the de Broglie wavelength of another electro

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must connect the accelerating voltage to momentum before taking the wavelength ratio.
questions.misconception: Treating wavelength as inversely proportional to voltage

explanation.body: In the non-relativistic model, the gain in kinetic energy is $e\Delta V=p^2/(2m)$, so $p=\sqrt{2me\Delta V}$. The de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda=h/p=h/\sqrt{2me\Delta V}$. Both electrons have the same mass and charge magnitude, so $\lambda_0/\lambda_1=\sqrt{100/1}=10$.

perOption.A: Inverts the wavelength ratio.
perOption.B: Treats the two momenta as equal despite the different accelerating voltages.
perOption.C: Correct. The ratio is the square root of the inverse voltage ratio.
perOption.D: Uses the voltage ratio directly and misses the square root.

perOption.B: Overestimates the photon frequency into the ultraviolet range.

The uncertainty in position of a particle in space is 2.00 x $10^{-20}$ m and the uncertainty in its momentum is 4.00 x $10^{-14}$ N s.

What is the minimum percentage change in uncertainty of momentum when the uncertainty in position is halved?
questions.stemText: The uncertainty in position of a particle in space is 2.00 x 10-20 m and the uncertainty in its momentum is 4.00 x 10-14 N s. What is the minimum percentage change in uncertainty of momentum when the uncertainty in position is halved? A - 100 % B - 66 % C 66 % D 100 %

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: Finds a new uncertainty bound and compares it with the initial value.
questions.misconception: Assuming the initial uncertainty is minimal

explanation.body: Using $\Delta x\Delta p\ge h$, halving $\Delta x$ gives $(1.00\times10^{-20})\Delta p\ge6.63\times10^{-34}$. The minimum $\Delta p$ is $6.63\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. The change is $\frac{6.63-4.00}{4.00}\times100\%\approx66\%$.

perOption.A: A 100% reduction would make the momentum uncertainty zero.
perOption.B: Reverses the sign even though the new minimum exceeds the original uncertainty.
perOption.C: Correct. The new minimum is about 66% higher.
perOption.D: Assumes the initial momentum uncertainty was already at its lower bound.

The graph below shows the variation of X-ray intensity with wavelength emitted from an X-ray tube.

[Intensity is plotted against wavelength. The continuous spectrum begins on the wavelength axis at $\lambda_1$, rises to a broad maximum, then falls. Two narrow peaks appear on the falling background. The first peak is marked $\lambda_2$ and the second is taller and at a longer wavelength.]

The target metal and the accelerating voltage are varied. Which wavelengths will be affected by the changes?

Options (changing the target metal, changing the accelerating voltage)
A $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_1$
B $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$
C $\lambda_2$, $\lambda_2$
D $\lambda_2$, $\lambda_1$

questions.difficultyReason: The student must distinguish the short-wavelength cutoff from the characteristic line on the same spectrum.
questions.misconception: Attributing the cutoff and characteristic peaks to the same cause

explanation.body: The minimum wavelength $\lambda_1$ occurs when an electron transfers all the kinetic energy it gained across the accelerating voltage to one X-ray photon in a single collision with a target atom. Changing the voltage therefore shifts $\lambda_1$. The peak at $\lambda_2$ comes from a characteristic energy-level difference in the target atoms, so changing the target metal shifts $\lambda_2$.

perOption.B: Swaps the controls for the cutoff and the characteristic peak.
perOption.C: Treats the characteristic peak wavelength as dependent on the accelerating voltage.
perOption.D: Correct. The target sets the characteristic line and the voltage sets the cutoff.

questions.stem:
To observe diffraction rings by a carbon film, a beam of electrons is accelerated from rest across a potential difference of V so that the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons is 1.0 x $10^{-10}$ m.

What is the value of V ?
questions.stemText: To observe diffraction rings by a carbon film, a beam of electrons is accelerated from rest across a potential difference of V so that the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons is 1.0 x 10-10 m. What is the value of V ? A 90 V B 150 V C 270 V D 330 V
questions.difficultyReason: The student must connect the de Broglie momentum to the kinetic energy gained across a potential difference.
questions.misconception: Confusing the de Broglie momentum relation with the energy gained per unit charge

explanation.body: From the de Broglie relation, $p=h/\lambda$. Conservation of energy gives $eV=\tfrac12 mv^2=p^2/(2m)$ for an electron starting from rest. Substituting gives $V=h^2/(2em\lambda^2)=(6.63\times10^{-34})^2/[2(1.60\times10^{-19})(9.11\times10^{-31})(1.0\times10^{-10})^2]\approx150\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the kinetic energy associated with the momentum fixed by the wavelength.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the kinetic energy by using too large a value for $p^2/(2m)$.
perOption.D: Overestimates the accelerating voltage by about a factor of two, consistent with dropping the factor of one-half in the kinetic energy.

questions.stem:
Two beams of monochromatic light have the same frequency. One beam has a greater intensity than the other beam.

How can the greater intensity of one beam be explained in terms of the particulate nature of light?
questions.stemText: Two beams of monochromatic light have the same frequency. One beam has a greater intensity than the other beam. How can the greater intensity of one beam be explained in terms of the particulate nature of light? A Each photon in the beam has more energy. B Each photon in the beam has greater speed. C The amplitude of oscillation is greater. D There are more photons passing through unit cross-sectional area of the beam per unit time.

options.label: A
options.text: Each photon in the beam has more energy.

options.label: B
options.text: Each photon in the beam has greater speed.

options.label: C
options.text: The amplitude of oscillation is greater.

options.label: D
options.text: There are more photons passing through unit cross-sectional area of the beam per unit time.

questions.difficultyReason: Standard photon-flux explanation of intensity.
questions.misconception: Linking intensity to photon energy or wave amplitude

explanation.body: Intensity equals the number of photons crossing unit area per unit time multiplied by the energy per photon. The beams have the same frequency, so their photons carry the same energy. The more intense beam therefore has more photons crossing unit area each second.

perOption.A: Equal frequencies give equal photon energies.
perOption.B: All photons travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
perOption.C: Amplitude describes the electric and magnetic field oscillations in the wave picture.
perOption.D: Correct.

Which diagram shows the positions where $\Delta y$ and $\Delta p$ in the equation above are defined and shows them in the correct direction? [Each option shows a slit on the left and a screen on the right.] A $\Delta y$ vertical at the slit, $\Delta p$ vertical at the slit B $\Delta y$ vertical at the screen, $\Delta p$ vertical at the screen C $\Delta y$ vertical at the slit, $\Delta p$ horizontal (along travel) at the slit D $\Delta y$ vertical at the screen, $\Delta p$ horizontal at the slit

questions.difficultyReason: Requires understanding which position and momentum components the slit constrains.
questions.misconception: Taking $\Delta p$ along the direction of travel or $\Delta y$ at the screen

explanation.body: The slit confines the electron in the transverse $y$ direction, so $\Delta y$ is defined at the slit. The electrons spread in $y$ as they pass through, giving a transverse momentum uncertainty $\Delta p_y$. The uncertainty principle pairs position and momentum along the same axis.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Places both uncertainties at the screen, although the slit sets the position uncertainty used here.
perOption.C: Pairs a transverse position uncertainty with longitudinal momentum uncertainty.
perOption.D: Uses the screen for the position uncertainty and pairs it with longitudinal momentum uncertainty.

questions.misconception: Scaling stopping voltage directly with photon energy

explanation.body: Einstein’s photoelectric equation is $hc/\lambda=\phi+eV_s$. Halving the wavelength doubles the photon energy. The same metal has the same work function $\phi$, so the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy and the stopping voltage both more than double.

perOption.A: Treats the drop in intensity as a drop in stopping voltage.
perOption.B: Overlooks the increase in photon energy when the wavelength is halved.
perOption.C: Doubles the stopping voltage as if the work function were zero.
perOption.D: Correct. The work function is subtracted just once from the doubled photon energy.

questions.stemText:
Evidence for the wave-particle duality may be observed by the diffraction of an electron beam at a slit. A diffraction pattern is observed on a suitable screen.

For an electron passing through the slit, the uncertainty in its position $\Delta x$ and the uncertainty in its momentum $\Delta p$ are related by the following expression

$\Delta p\Delta x\ge h$

Which diagram below shows the positions where $\Delta x$ and $\Delta p$ in the equation above are defined and shows them in the correct direction?

[All diagrams show a slit at left, a screen at right and a dashed horizontal beam axis.]
A [Both arrows point up at the slit, with $\Delta x$ above the beam axis and $\Delta p$ below it.]
B [Both arrows point up at the screen, with $\Delta x$ above the beam axis and $\Delta p$ below it.]

questions.difficultyReason: Students must identify both the location of the position constraint and the matching momentum component.
questions.misconception: Pairing position and momentum uncertainties along different axes

explanation.body: The electron’s transverse position is constrained at the slit, where diffraction occurs. The uncertainty principle pairs $\Delta x$ with the momentum uncertainty $\Delta p$ in that same transverse direction at the slit.

perOption.A: Correct. Both uncertainties are transverse and shown at the slit.
perOption.B: Uses the screen as the location of the position constraint.
perOption.C: Pairs transverse position uncertainty with longitudinal momentum uncertainty.

questions.stem: Heisenberg’s Uncertainty Principle is a consequence of
questions.stemText: Heisenberg’s Uncertainty Principle is a consequence of A the wave-particle duality of physical entities. B the existence of discrete energy levels in atoms. C relativistic effects as particles move at speeds close to the speed of light. D the fact that all measuring instruments have a minimum resolution which limits their precision.

perOption.B: Attributes the uncertainty to discrete atomic energies, although it also applies to free particles.
perOption.C: Attributes the uncertainty to relativity, although it also applies at low speeds.

questions.stemText:
When a beam of light of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident normally on a plane mirror, it is reflected totally. The intensity of the light corresponds to a rate of $n$ photons per second.

Which of the following expressions gives the force exerted on the mirror by the beam of light?

A $nh\lambda$
B $\frac{nh}{\lambda}$
C $2nh\lambda$
D $\frac{2nh}{\lambda}$

stemImage.alt: Question 27: When a beam of light of wavelength 휆 is incident normally on a plane mirror, it is reflected totally. The intensity of the light corresponds to a rate of n phot

questions.difficultyReason: Requires calculating the momentum change on reflection and turning it into a rate.
questions.misconception: Treating reflection like absorption.

explanation.body:
A photon of wavelength $\lambda$ has momentum of magnitude $p=h/\lambda$. Reflection reverses that momentum, transferring $2h/\lambda$ to the mirror per photon.

By Newton’s second law, the force is the rate of momentum transfer, $F=n(2h/\lambda)=2nh/\lambda$.

perOption.A: Multiplies by wavelength and omits the factor of two from reflection.
perOption.B: Counts the momentum transfer for absorption instead of reversal.
perOption.C: Multiplies by wavelength when finding the photon momentum.
perOption.D: Correct. Each reflected photon transfers $2h/\lambda$ of momentum.

questions.stemText:

What is the work function of the metal cathode?

A $2.9\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$
B $3.1\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$
C $3.5\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$
D $3.9\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$

stemImage.alt: Question 28: The metal cathode of a photocell is illuminated by light quanta of energy 3.5 × 10-19 J each. By applying a stopping potential of 0.25 V, the current through th

questions.difficultyReason: Requires converting the stopping potential into a maximum kinetic energy before subtracting.
questions.misconception: Adding the stopping energy to the photon energy.

explanation.body:
The photoelectric energy equation is $E_{\mathrm{photon}}=\phi+eV_s$. Substituting gives $3.5\times10^{-19}=\phi+(1.6\times10^{-19})(0.25)$ in joules.

Thus $\phi=3.1\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts more than the stopping energy $eV_s$.
perOption.B: Correct. The work function is the photon energy minus $eV_s$.
perOption.C: Ignores the kinetic energy implied by the nonzero stopping potential.
perOption.D: Adds $eV_s$ to the photon energy.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The photoelectric effect refers to the phenomenon that electrons may be ejected from a metal surface when light falls on the surface.

Which of the following statements about the photoelectric effect is correct?
questions.stemText: The photoelectric effect refers to the phenomenon that electrons may be ejected from a metal surface when light falls on the surface. Which of the following statements about the photoelectric effect is correct? A The maximum energy of the electrons is independent of the type of metal. B The maximum energy of the electrons is independent of the intensity of the incident light. C The waves associated with the electrons have the same wavelength as the incident light. D Electrons are ejected only if the wavelength of the incident light is greater than some minimum value.

options.label: A
options.text: The maximum energy of the electrons is independent of the type of metal.

options.label: B
options.text: The maximum energy of the electrons is independent of the intensity of the incident light.

options.label: C
options.text: The waves associated with the electrons have the same wavelength as the incident light.

options.label: D
options.text: Electrons are ejected only if the wavelength of the incident light is greater than some minimum value.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing photon energy from the number of photons arriving each second.
questions.misconception: Brighter light gives each emitted electron more energy.

explanation.body: The photoelectric equation is $hc/\lambda=\phi+K_{\max}$. At a fixed wavelength, changing the intensity changes how many photons strike the metal per second while each photon still carries energy $hc/\lambda$. The maximum electron kinetic energy therefore stays the same.

perOption.A: Different metals can have different work functions, which affect the maximum kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Correct. At fixed wavelength, intensity changes the photon arrival rate.
perOption.C: The electron’s de Broglie wavelength depends on its own momentum.
perOption.D: Emission requires a sufficiently high frequency, so the threshold is a maximum wavelength.

explanation.body: The de Broglie relation $\lambda=h/(mv)$ gives $v=h/(m\lambda)$. At a fixed wavelength, speed is inversely proportional to mass. The helium-4 nucleus has the largest mass, so it has the smallest speed.

perOption.A: A proton is lighter than the helium-4 nucleus and must move faster.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The electron has the smallest mass and requires the greatest speed.
perOption.D: A neutron is lighter than the helium-4 nucleus and must move faster.

A $nh\lambda$ B $\dfrac{nh}{\lambda}$ C $2nh\lambda$ D $\dfrac{2nh}{\lambda}$

questions.difficultyReason: Combines photon momentum with rate of change of momentum, including the factor of 2 on reflection.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the factor of 2 for reflection, or using $p = h\lambda$

explanation.body: Each photon has momentum of magnitude $p=h/\lambda$. Total reflection reverses that momentum, so the change in momentum has magnitude $p-(-p)=2h/\lambda$. At $n$ photons per second, the force on the mirror is the rate of momentum transfer, $2nh/\lambda$.

perOption.A: Multiplies by $\lambda$ instead of dividing and omits the factor of two from reflection.
perOption.B: Counts only the incident momentum, as for absorption.
perOption.C: Accounts for the reversal but multiplies by wavelength instead of dividing.

questions.difficultyReason: Standard photoelectric fact: intensity affects photon rate only.
questions.misconception: Believing light intensity changes the threshold frequency or electron energy

explanation.body: The threshold frequency depends on the minimum energy required to release an electron from europium, which is independent of light intensity. At the same frequency, higher intensity means more photons reach the metal per unit time, so more electrons are emitted per unit time.

perOption.A: Incorrectly lowers the threshold and overlooks the increase in photon arrival rate.
perOption.B: Incorrectly lowers the threshold frequency when only intensity changes.
perOption.C: Overlooks the increase in electron emission rate as more photons arrive each second.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stemText: A student is given a gold-leaf electroscope and two light sources of wavelength 450 nm (blue) and 650 nm (red) to investigate the photoelectric effect of potassium and aluminium. She places the metal on the electroscope, neutralises it, and shines one of the lights on the metal. If the metal emits electrons, the gold leaf rises. [Diagram: gold-leaf electroscope with metal disc on top, metal under test placed on the disc, light incident on it.] Minimum energy to release electrons: potassium 2.3 eV, aluminium 4.3 eV. Which gives the correct observation? [Table: potassium red / potassium blue / aluminium red / aluminium blue] A does not rise / rise / does not rise / rise B does not rise / rise / does not rise / does not rise C rise / does not rise / rise / rise D rise / does not rise / rise / does not rise

stemImage.alt: Question 28: A student is given a gold-leaf electroscope and two light sources of wavelength 450 nm (blue light) and 650 nm (red light) to investigate the photoelectric effe

questions.difficultyReason: Convert both wavelengths to photon energies and compare against two work functions in an unfamiliar electroscope setup.
questions.misconception: Thinking shorter wavelength light always causes emission regardless of work function

explanation.body: When electrons escape, the electroscope becomes positively charged and the gold leaf rises. Using $E=hc/\lambda$, a red photon has energy $1.9125\ \mathrm{eV}$, below both work functions. A blue photon has energy $2.7625\ \mathrm{eV}$, above potassium’s work function but below aluminium’s, so the leaf rises only for potassium under blue light.

perOption.A: Assumes blue photons can also overcome aluminium’s $4.3\ \mathrm{eV}$ work function.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reverses the predictions for potassium and assumes both photon energies exceed aluminium’s work function.
perOption.D: Reverses the predictions for potassium and incorrectly treats red photons as energetic enough for aluminium.

questions.stemText: A green laser pointer and a red laser pointer of the same power cast circular images on a white screen of the same diameter. The wavelengths of the green and red lasers are $\lambda_G$ and $\lambda_R$ respectively. [Diagram: two equal-sized circular spots labelled green and red.] If the pressure exerted by the green laser on the screen is $p$, what is the pressure exerted by the red laser? A $p$ B $\frac{\lambda_G}{\lambda_R}p$ C $\frac{\lambda_R}{\lambda_G}p$ D $\left(\frac{\lambda_G}{\lambda_R}\right)^2 p$

stemImage.alt: Question 27: A green laser pointer and a red laser pointer of the same power cast circular images on a white screen of the same diameter. The wavelengths of the green and re

questions.difficultyReason: Needs realising photon momentum and photon rate both depend on wavelength and cancel.
questions.misconception: Thinking pressure depends on photon momentum alone, not the photon rate

explanation.body: Each photon has momentum $h/\lambda$ and energy $hc/\lambda$, so a beam of power $P$ delivers $P/(hc/\lambda)$ photons per second. Assuming complete reflection, each photon’s momentum reverses, giving a force of $2P/c$ on the photons and an equal force magnitude on the screen. Dividing by the spot area $\pi D^2/4$ gives $8P/(c\pi D^2)$. The two beams have equal power and spot diameter, so the red beam also exerts pressure $p$.

perOption.A: Uses the momentum ratio of individual photons and overlooks the higher photon rate for red light.
perOption.B: Correct. The wavelength factors cancel.
perOption.C: Uses the photon-rate ratio and overlooks the lower momentum per red photon.
perOption.D: Squares the per-photon momentum ratio even though the force is the photon rate times the momentum change.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which statement best describes the 'electron cloud' in an atom?
questions.stemText: Which statement best describes the 'electron cloud' in an atom? A A shell of negative charge at a fixed radius. B A region where the electron's charge is uniformly distributed. C The path the electron follows around the nucleus. D A region where the probability of finding the electron is high.

options.label: A
options.text: A shell of negative charge at a fixed radius.

options.label: B
options.text: A region where the electron's charge is uniformly distributed.

options.label: C
options.text: The path the electron follows around the nucleus.

options.label: D
options.text: A region where the probability of finding the electron is high.

questions.difficultyReason: Direct recall of the probabilistic interpretation of the wavefunction.
questions.misconception: Picturing the electron as following a definite orbit

explanation.body: The electron’s state is represented by a wavefunction $\psi$. Its squared magnitude $|\psi|^2$ is the probability density, and the electron cloud visualises where the electron is likely to be found.

perOption.A: Confines the electron to a single radius even though its probability density extends over a region.
perOption.B: Assumes a uniform charge distribution even though the probability density varies with position.
perOption.C: Treats the electron cloud as a classical trajectory.
perOption.D: Correct. The cloud shows where the electron is likely to be found.

questions.stemText:
An electron is in the $n=2$ quantum state of a one-dimensional box with kinetic energy of $6.0\ \mathrm{eV}$.

A proton is in the $n=3$ quantum state of another one-dimensional box with kinetic energy of $0.20\ \mathrm{eV}$.

explanation.body: From $E=n^2h^2/(8mL^2)$, $L=\sqrt{n^2h^2/(8mE)}\propto n/\sqrt{mE}$. Thus $L_e/L_p=(n_e/n_p)\sqrt{m_pE_p/(m_eE_e)}=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{\frac{(1.67\times10^{-27})(0.20)}{(9.11\times10^{-31})(6.0)}}=5.2113\approx5.2$.

questions.stemText:
An electron is confined within an atom.

What is the order of magnitude of the minimum uncertainty in its momentum?

A. $10^{-48}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$
B. $10^{-24}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$
C. $10^{-20}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$
D. $10^{-15}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recalling the atomic length scale and using it to estimate the momentum uncertainty.
questions.misconception: Using a nuclear length scale for an atom

explanation.body: The diameter of an atom is about $10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$, so take $\Delta x\approx10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$. Using $\Delta x\,\Delta p\gtrsim h$, the minimum momentum uncertainty is of order $h/\Delta x\sim10^{-34}/10^{-10}=10^{-24}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

perOption.A: Implies a position uncertainty vastly larger than the atom.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Assumes confinement to a much smaller distance than an atomic diameter.
perOption.D: Uses a momentum scale that would require far tighter confinement than even a nuclear diameter.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two electrons are confined along a horizontal axis. The uncertainty in the position of electron A is 0.20 nm, while the uncertainty in the position of electron B is 0.50 nm.

What is the ratio of the minimum uncertainty in the momentum of electron A to that of electron B?
questions.stemText: Two electrons are confined along a horizontal axis. The uncertainty in the position of electron A is 0.20 nm, while the uncertainty in the position of electron B is 0.50 nm. What is the ratio of the minimum uncertainty in the momentum of electron A to that of electron B? A 0.40 B 0.70 C 1.5 D 2.5
questions.difficultyReason: Use the inverse relationship and keep the order of the ratio straight.
questions.misconception: Treating the two uncertainties as directly proportional

explanation.body: At the minimum momentum uncertainty, both electrons have the same position–momentum uncertainty product, so $\Delta x_A\Delta p_A=\Delta x_B\Delta p_B$. Thus $\Delta p_A/\Delta p_B=\Delta x_B/\Delta x_A=0.50/0.20=2.5$.

perOption.A: This takes the ratio of position uncertainties in the same order as the requested momentum ratio.
perOption.B: This puts the momentum ratio below one even though A has the tighter position constraint.
perOption.C: This is close to taking the square root of the inverse position ratio, but the relation is directly inverse.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: What is the de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass m and kinetic energy E?
questions.stemText: What is the de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass m and kinetic energy E? A h 2 mE B 2mE h C h mE D h 2 mE
questions.difficultyReason: Express momentum in terms of kinetic energy before substituting into the de Broglie equation.
questions.misconception: Inverting the de Broglie relation or dropping the kinetic energy factor of one half

explanation.body: The kinetic energy is $E=\tfrac12mv^2=(mv)^2/(2m)=p^2/(2m)$, so $p=\sqrt{2mE}$. The de Broglie relation then gives $\lambda=h/p=h/\sqrt{2mE}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: This gives the inverse wavelength $p/h$.
perOption.C: This drops the factor of two when rearranging $E=p^2/(2m)$.
perOption.D: This multiplies Planck’s constant by the momentum instead of dividing by it.

questions.misconception: Counting only transitions to the ground state

The four accessible levels give six possible downward transitions, so at most six emission lines can be observed.

perOption.A: Assumes excitation requires the incident electron to give up its entire kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Counts only three transitions, for example those ending at the ground state.

questions.stemText:
When electrons with velocity $v$ travel through a vacuum and are incident on a thin carbon film, they produce a pattern of concentric circles on the fluorescent screen.

What causes the pattern and how would the pattern change when the velocity $v$ is decreased?
| | cause | change to pattern |
| A | refraction | diameters of circles decrease |
| B | refraction | diameters of circles increase |
| C | diffraction | diameters of circles decrease |
| D | diffraction | diameters of circles increase |

stemImage.alt: Question 27: When electrons with velocity v travel through a vacuum and are incident on a thin carbon film, they produce a pattern of concentric circles on the fluorescent s

questions.difficultyReason: Standard electron diffraction fact plus $\lambda=h/p$.
questions.misconception: Thinks slower electrons have shorter wavelength.

explanation.body:
When the electron velocity decreases, the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda = h/p$ increases.

The pattern is caused by diffraction, and the diffraction angle satisfies $\sin\theta \propto \lambda$, so $\sin\theta$ increases and the circles have larger diameter.

perOption.A: Wrong cause (refraction) and wrong change.
perOption.B: Wrong cause: electrons passing through a carbon film diffract.
perOption.C: Correct cause but the wrong change: smaller $v$ means larger $\lambda$, so larger circles.
perOption.D: Correct. Diffraction; diameters increase.

questions.stem:
Light quanta each of energy 3.5 x $10^{-19}$ J fall on the cathode of a photocell. The current through the cell is just reduced to zero by applying a reverse voltage to make the cathode 0.25 V positive with respect to the anode.

The minimum energy required to remove an electron from the cathode is
questions.stemText: Light quanta each of energy 3.5 x 10-19 J fall on the cathode of a photocell. The current through the cell is just reduced to zero by applying a reverse voltage to make the cathode 0.25 V positive with respect to the anode. The minimum energy required to remove an electron from the cathode is A 2.9 x $10^{-19}$ J B 3.1 x $10^{-19}$ J C 3.5 x $10^{-19}$ J D 3.9 x $10^{-19}$ J
questions.difficultyReason: One-step use of the photoelectric equation, with the stopping potential converted to joules.
questions.misconception: Taking the photon energy as the work function

explanation.body:
Einstein's photoelectric equation with the stopping potential: $hf = \Phi + eV_s$.

$3.5\times10^{-19} = \Phi + (1.6\times10^{-19})(0.25)$, so $\Phi = 3.1\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts 0.25 eV twice (or adds wrongly); not the work function.
perOption.B: Correct. The stopping energy is $0.25\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.4\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.
perOption.C: Ignores the stopping potential and takes the photon energy as the work function.
perOption.D: Adds $eV_s$ to the photon energy instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Electrons and protons in two beams are travelling at the same speed. The beams are diffracted by objects of the same size. Which correctly compares the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda_e$ of the electrons with the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda_p$ of the protons and the width of the diffraction patterns that are produced by these beams? [Table] A: $\lambda_e<\lambda_p$; electron beam width > proton beam width. B: $\lambda_e<\lambda_p$; electron beam width < proton beam width. C: $\lambda_e>\lambda_p$; electron beam width > proton beam width. D: $\lambda_e>\lambda_p$; electron beam width < proton beam width.

stemImage.alt: Question 26: Electrons and protons in two beams are travelling at the same speed. The beams are diffracted by objects of the same size. Which correctly compares the de Brogl

questions.difficultyReason: Two linked qualitative steps: de Broglie wavelength vs mass, then wavelength vs diffraction width.
questions.misconception: Thinking heavier particles diffract more

explanation.body:
$\lambda = h/mv$, so $\lambda \propto 1/m$ at the same speed $v$. The electron mass is much smaller than the proton mass, so $\lambda_e > \lambda_p$.

For single-slit diffraction, $b\sin\theta = \lambda$, so $\sin\theta \propto \lambda$. The diffraction angle (pattern width) for electrons is much larger than for protons.

perOption.A: Wrong wavelength comparison: smaller mass gives longer wavelength.
perOption.B: Wrong on both: electrons have the longer wavelength and wider pattern.
perOption.C: Correct. $\lambda_e > \lambda_p$ and wider electron pattern.
perOption.D: Right wavelength comparison but a longer wavelength gives a wider, not narrower, pattern.

[Diagram: photocell with plate M, variable supply and microammeter in series.] What is the ratio (number of electrons emitted per unit time)/(number of photons incident per unit time)? questions.misconception: Forgetting to convert photon energy from eV to J

explanation.body:
Electrons per second: $dN_e/dt = I/e = 2.0\times10^{-6}/1.6\times10^{-19}$.

Photons per second: $dN_p/dt = P/E = 0.31\times10^{-3}/(3.11\times1.6\times10^{-19})$.

questions.stemText: An electron moves with a constant velocity of $1.5\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. If its momentum is measured to a precision of 0.2%, what is the uncertainty associated with its position? A: $1.2\times10^{-9}$ m. B: $2.4\times10^{-9}$ m. C: $2.4\times10^{-7}$ m. D: $1.2\times10^{-6}$ m.

questions.misconception: Using 0.2 instead of 0.002 for 0.2%

perOption.B: Wrong power of ten and prefactor.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An X-ray spectrum is shown in the diagram below.

What does the value of $\lambda _{\mathrm{min}}$ represent?
questions.stemText: An X-ray spectrum is shown in the diagram below. intensity λmin wavelength What does the value of λmin represent? A The threshold wavelength of the target metal used to produce X-ray. B The wavelength corresponding to the ionization energy of the target metal. C The de Broglie wavelength of the electron with maximum energy. D The wavelength corresponding to all the energy supplied to an electron in the accelerating electric field being converted into a single X-ray photon.

options.label: A
options.text: The threshold wavelength of the target metal used to produce X-ray.

options.label: B
options.text: The wavelength corresponding to the ionization energy of the target metal.

options.label: C
options.text: The de Broglie wavelength of the electron with maximum energy.

options.label: D
options.text: The wavelength corresponding to all the energy supplied to an electron in the accelerating electric field being converted into a single X-ray photon.

questions.difficultyReason: A standard definition of the cut-off wavelength in the X-ray spectrum.
questions.misconception: Confusing the X-ray cut-off wavelength with a threshold wavelength or the electron's de Broglie wavelength.

explanation.body:
The school's key prints only the letter D for this question.

The continuous X-ray spectrum has a sharp cut-off at $\lambda_{min}$. This occurs when an electron gives up all its kinetic energy $eV$ in a single collision, producing one photon of the maximum energy: $eV = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{min}}$.

perOption.A: The threshold wavelength belongs to photoelectric emission, not X-ray production.
perOption.B: The cut-off depends on the accelerating voltage, not on the ionisation energy of the target.
perOption.C: It is a photon wavelength, not the electron's de Broglie wavelength.
perOption.D: Correct. All the electron's energy goes into one photon.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an alpha particle of kinetic energy E, given that u is the unified atomic mass unit?
questions.stemText: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an alpha particle of kinetic energy E, given that u is the unified atomic mass unit? A h 2 uE B 2 uE h C h 2 2 uE D 2 2uE h
questions.difficultyReason: Needs p from kinetic energy, the mass of an alpha particle as 4u and simplification of the root.
questions.misconception: Using the mass of one nucleon instead of an alpha particle (4u).

explanation.body:
$E = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so $p = \sqrt{2mE}$.

The mass of an alpha particle is $4u$, so $p = \sqrt{8uE}$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{8uE}} = \dfrac{h}{2\sqrt{2uE}}$.

perOption.A: Uses mass $u$ instead of $4u$, or drops a factor of 2 inside the root.
perOption.B: Inverted: wavelength is $h/p$, not $p/h$.
perOption.C: Correct. $h/\sqrt{8uE}$.
perOption.D: Inverted: wavelength is $h/p$, not $p/h$.

questions.stemText:
A proton has a kinetic energy of $1.00\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

If its momentum is measured with an uncertainty of $1.0\%$, what is the minimum uncertainty in its position?

A $1.22\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$
B $2.87\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$
C $9.08\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$
D $6.59\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$

stemImage.alt: Question 29: A proton has a kinetic energy of 1.00 MeV. If its momentum is measured with an uncertainty of 1.0 %, what is the minimum uncertainty in its position?

questions.difficultyReason: Students must convert the energy, calculate the momentum and apply the percentage uncertainty.
questions.misconception: The full momentum can be substituted for its uncertainty.

explanation.body: Using $K=p^2/(2m)$ with $K=(1.00\times10^6)(1.6\times10^{-19})\ \mathrm{J}$ and $m=1.67\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$ gives $p=2.312\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. The momentum uncertainty is $\Delta p=0.01p=2.312\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. Using the syllabus estimate $\Delta p\,\Delta x\approx h$, the minimum position uncertainty is approximately $2.87\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Is about $\sqrt{10}$ too large, consistent with a factor-of-ten underestimate of the energy in the momentum calculation.
perOption.D: Implies a momentum uncertainty larger than the full proton momentum under the syllabus estimate.

The experiment is repeated with a metal Y of a larger work function.
Which of the following shows the graph for Y?

B [Y is parallel to X but with a larger $f$-intercept]
C [Y has a smaller $f$-intercept and a steeper gradient than X]

questions.difficultyReason: Standard interpretation of the photoelectric $E_{max}$–$f$ graph's gradient and intercept.
questions.misconception: thinking the gradient depends on the metal

explanation.body:
From $hf = \phi + E_{max}$, $E_{max} = hf - hf_0$.

The $x$-intercept is the threshold frequency $f_0 = \phi/h$, so a larger work function gives a larger threshold frequency: Y's line starts further right. The gradient of the graph is Planck's constant, so it does not change and the lines are parallel.

perOption.A: Shows a smaller threshold frequency, which corresponds to a smaller work function.
perOption.B: Correct. Larger $f_0$, same gradient $h$.
perOption.C: Shows a smaller threshold frequency and a steeper gradient; the gradient must stay $h$.
perOption.D: Has the larger threshold frequency but a smaller gradient; the gradient must stay $h$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The speed of an electron is measured to be 5.8 × $10^{6}$ m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ to an accuracy of 0.2%.

What is the minimum uncertainty in determining the position of the electron?
questions.stemText: The speed of an electron is measured to be 5.8 × 106 m s-1 to an accuracy of 0.2%. What is the minimum uncertainty in determining the position of the electron? A 5.7 × $10^{-38}$ m B 1.1 × $10^{-26}$ m C 1.3 × $10^{-10}$ m D 6.3 × $10^{-8}$ m
questions.difficultyReason: Two-step substitution into $\Delta p = m\Delta v$ and the uncertainty principle.
questions.misconception: using the full momentum instead of its uncertainty

explanation.body:
Uncertainty in momentum: $\Delta p = m\Delta v = (9.11\times10^{-31})(5.8\times10^{6})\left(\dfrac{0.2}{100}\right) = 1.0568\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

Using $\Delta p\,\Delta x \geq h$: $\Delta x_{min} = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{1.0568\times10^{-26}} = 6.3\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Divides $h$ by $\Delta v$ only, omitting the electron mass.
perOption.B: This is $\Delta p$, not $\Delta x$.
perOption.C: Uses the full momentum $mv$ (giving the de Broglie wavelength) instead of the uncertainty $\Delta p$.
perOption.D: Correct. $\Delta x = h/\Delta p$ with $\Delta p = 0.2\%$ of $mv$.

questions.stemText:
An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference to achieve a final kinetic energy of $9.3 \times 10^{-16}$ J.

What is the de Broglie wavelength of the electron after being accelerated through this potential difference?

A $5.1 \times 10^{-10}$ m
B $1.6 \times 10^{-11}$ m
C $5.1 \times 10^{-12}$ m
D $3.6 \times 10^{-19}$ m

stemImage.alt: Question 27: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference to achieve a final kinetic energy of 9.3  10–16 J. What is the de Broglie wavelength of the

questions.difficultyReason: Standard two-step calculation from kinetic energy to momentum to de Broglie wavelength.
questions.misconception: Using the photon relation $\lambda = hc/E$ for an electron

explanation.body:
Find the speed from the kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 9.3 \times 10^{-16}$, so $\frac{1}{2}(9.11 \times 10^{-31})v^2 = 9.3 \times 10^{-16}$, giving $v = 4.52 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Then $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{(9.11 \times 10^{-31})(4.52 \times 10^{7})} = 1.6 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Too large by a factor of about 30; does not follow from $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2mE_k}$ with the given energy.
perOption.B: Correct. $\lambda = h/mv$ with $v$ found from the kinetic energy.
perOption.C: Off by a factor of about 3; arises from a slip such as omitting the factor 2 or the square root in $p = \sqrt{2mE_k}$.
perOption.D: Treats the electron like a photon, using $\lambda = hc/E$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
When an electron beam passes through a slit, a diffraction pattern is observed on a suitable screen. This phenomenon can be explained using Heisenberg position-momentum uncertainty principle.

[Diagram: an electron beam travels in the $x$-direction (to the right) through a slit of width 7.2 nm; the slit width is measured along the $y$-direction (vertical). Axes show $y$ up and $x$ to the right. A screen on the right is labelled 'screen where diffraction pattern is observed'.]

The slit width is 7.2 nm.

For an electron passing through the slit, what is the uncertainty in the momentum of the electron and its direction that best relates to the phenomenon?

| | uncertainty in momentum / kg m s$^{-1}$ | direction |
|---|---|---|
| A | $9.2 \times 10^{-35}$ | $x$ |
| B | $9.2 \times 10^{-35}$ | $y$ |
| C | $9.2 \times 10^{-26}$ | $x$ |
| D | $9.2 \times 10^{-26}$ | $y$ |

stemImage.alt: Question 28: When an electron beam passes through a slit, a diffraction pattern is observed on a suitable screen. This phenomenon can be explained using Heisenberg position-

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation is one line, but students must recognise that the momentum uncertainty is along the slit width, perpendicular to the beam.
questions.misconception: Momentum uncertainty is along the direction of travel

explanation.body:
Use $\Delta x \Delta p \approx h$: $(7.2 \times 10^{-9})(\Delta p) \approx 6.63 \times 10^{-34}$, so $\Delta p \approx 9.2 \times 10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

The uncertainty in position is the slit width, which lies along the $y$-direction, so the uncertainty in momentum is also in the $y$-direction. This sideways spread in momentum is what spreads the electrons out into a diffraction pattern.

perOption.A: Wrong magnitude (a powers-of-ten slip with the nm) and wrong direction: the slit width is along $y$, not $x$.
perOption.B: Right direction, but the magnitude comes from a powers-of-ten slip when converting 7.2 nm.
perOption.C: Right magnitude, but the position uncertainty (slit width) is along $y$, so $\Delta p$ is along $y$, not along the beam.
perOption.D: Correct. $\Delta p \approx h/\Delta y$, perpendicular to the beam.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An electron and a proton are both accelerated from rest through the same electric potential difference.

Which row correctly compares the kinetic energy and the de Broglie wavelength of the electron and proton after the acceleration?

Option | kinetic energy | de Broglie wavelength
A | electron has greater energy | proton has longer wavelength
B | proton has greater energy | electron has longer wavelength
C | both have the same energy | proton has longer wavelength
D | both have the same energy | electron has longer wavelength

stemImage.alt: Question 28: An electron and a proton are both accelerated from rest through the same electric potential difference. Which row correctly compares the kinetic energy and the

questions.difficultyReason: The comparison links energy gained through a potential difference to momentum and wavelength.
questions.misconception: Assuming equal kinetic energies imply equal momenta.

explanation.body: Both particles start from rest and gain kinetic energy $K=|q||\Delta V|$. The charge magnitudes and the magnitudes of the potential differences are equal, giving equal kinetic energies. Combining $\lambda=h/p$ with $p^2/(2m)=K$ gives $\lambda=h/\sqrt{2m|q||\Delta V|}$. The heavier proton therefore has the shorter wavelength.

perOption.A: Assigns the electron more energy and reverses the wavelength comparison.
perOption.B: Assigns the proton more energy even though both particles gain equal energy.
perOption.C: Reverses the momentum comparison at fixed kinetic energy.
perOption.D: Correct. The lighter electron has the longer wavelength.

questions.misconception: Treating the signed wavefunction as probability density.

explanation.body: Squaring the magnitude of the wavefunction gives the probability density, $|\psi|^2$. The wavefunction has its largest magnitude at Q and S, so the probability density is highest at both positions.

perOption.A: Counts the positive peak but misses the equally large magnitude at the negative trough.
perOption.B: Correct. The squared magnitude is maximal at Q and S.
perOption.C: Includes P and R, where the wavefunction is zero.
perOption.D: Selects the nodes, where the probability density is zero.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A proton has a kinetic energy of $1.00\ \mathrm{MeV}$. If its momentum is measured with an uncertainty of $1.00\%$, what is the minimum uncertainty in its position?

A $4.14\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{m}$
B $1.15\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{m}$
C $2.87\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$
D $1.99\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m}$

stemImage.alt: Question 28: A proton has a kinetic energy of 1.00 MeV. If its momentum is measured with an uncertainty of 1.00 %, what is the minimum uncertainty in its position?

questions.difficultyReason: Convert the proton energy to joules, calculate its momentum uncertainty, and apply the syllabus uncertainty relation.
questions.misconception: Using the full momentum or the percentage alone for momentum uncertainty.

explanation.body: From $E=p^2/(2m)$, the proton momentum is $p=\sqrt{2mE}=\sqrt{2(1.67\times10^{-27})(1.00\times10^6)(1.6\times10^{-19})}=2.3117\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. The $1.00\%$ uncertainty gives $\Delta p=2.3117\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. Using the syllabus estimate $\Delta x\,\Delta p\gtrsim h$, the minimum is about $h/\Delta p=2.87\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses a momentum uncertainty far larger than the stated 1.00% when substituted into $h/\Delta p$.
perOption.B: Also implies a momentum uncertainty far larger than 1.00% of the calculated momentum.
perOption.C: Correct. This is the result with the syllabus uncertainty estimate.
perOption.D: Implies a smaller momentum uncertainty than the stated 1.00%.

questions.stem: What provides evidence for the particulate nature of electromagnetic radiation?
questions.stemText: What provides evidence for the particulate nature of electromagnetic radiation? A Electrons can be diffracted by a carbon film. B Light can be diffracted by an obstacle. C Light from two coherent sources can produce an interference pattern. D Photoelectric emission occurs only for incident radiation frequencies above a minimum frequency.

options.label: A
options.text: Electrons can be diffracted by a carbon film.

options.label: B
options.text: Light can be diffracted by an obstacle.

options.label: C
options.text: Light from two coherent sources can produce an interference pattern.

options.label: D
options.text: Photoelectric emission occurs only for incident radiation frequencies above a minimum frequency.

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: A standard recall of wave versus particle evidence.
questions.misconception: Confusing evidence for the wave nature of particles with evidence for the particle nature of light

explanation.body:
(A) Electron diffraction is evidence for the wave nature of particles.

(B) and (C) Diffraction and interference of light are evidence for the wave nature of electromagnetic radiation.

(D) A threshold frequency for photoelectric emission is evidence for the particulate (photon) nature of electromagnetic radiation.

perOption.A: Electron diffraction shows the wave nature of particles, not the particle nature of radiation.
perOption.B: Diffraction is evidence for the wave nature of electromagnetic radiation.
perOption.C: Interference is evidence for the wave nature of electromagnetic radiation.
perOption.D: Correct. The threshold frequency shows that energy arrives in photons of $hf$.

questions.stemText: Electrons are only just emitted from a metal surface when illuminated with light of frequency $4.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz. When illuminated with light of frequency $f$, the stopping potential is found to be 1.5 V. What is the value of the frequency $f$? A $3.8 \times 10^{13}$ Hz B $3.6 \times 10^{14}$ Hz C $4.2 \times 10^{14}$ Hz D $7.6 \times 10^{14}$ Hz

questions.difficultyReason: A direct use of the photoelectric equation, with the work function given as a threshold frequency.

explanation.body:
$E_p = \Phi + KE_\mathrm{max}$, where the work function is $\Phi = hf_0$ and $KE_\mathrm{max} = eV_s$.

$6.63\times10^{-34} f = (6.63\times10^{-34})(4.0\times10^{14}) + (1.6\times10^{-19})(1.5)$

$f = 7.6\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$

perOption.A: A power-of-ten or arithmetic slip; $f$ must exceed the threshold of $4.0\times10^{14}$ Hz.
perOption.B: This is only the $eV_s/h$ term. It omits the threshold frequency.
perOption.C: Too small an increase above the threshold for a 1.5 V stopping potential, likely from a unit slip with eV.
perOption.D: Correct. $f = f_0 + eV_s/h$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: In the photoelectric effect, light incident on a metal surface causes electrons to be ejected from the surface. Which statement is correct?
questions.stemText: In the photoelectric effect, light incident on a metal surface causes electrons to be ejected from the surface. Which statement is correct? A Electrons are ejected only if the wavelength of the incident light is greater than some minimum value. B The de Broglie wavelength of the ejected electrons is the same as the wavelength of the incident light. C The maximum energy of the electrons is independent of the intensity of the incident light. D The maximum energy of the electrons is independent of the type of metal.

options.label: A
options.text: Electrons are ejected only if the wavelength of the incident light is greater than some minimum value.

options.label: B
options.text: The de Broglie wavelength of the ejected electrons is the same as the wavelength of the incident light.

options.label: C
options.text: The maximum energy of the electrons is independent of the intensity of the incident light.

options.label: D
options.text: The maximum energy of the electrons is independent of the type of metal.

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Standard photoelectric facts that are drilled heavily.
questions.misconception: Threshold condition stated as a minimum wavelength instead of a maximum

explanation.body:
The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, $hf - \Phi$, depends only on the frequency of the light and the metal, not on the intensity, so C is correct.

A is wrong: electrons are ejected only if the wavelength is smaller than some maximum value. B is wrong: the de Broglie wavelength of the ejected electrons is not the same as the wavelength of the incident light. D is wrong: the maximum energy depends on the type of metal.

perOption.A: Reversed: electrons are ejected only if the wavelength is smaller than some maximum (threshold) value.
perOption.B: The de Broglie wavelength of the ejected electrons is not the same as the wavelength of the incident light.
perOption.C: Correct. Intensity changes only the number of photoelectrons, not their maximum energy.
perOption.D: The maximum energy depends on the type of metal through its work function.

questions.stemText:
The diagram shows a sketch of the X-ray spectrum produced when electrons strike a metal target.

[Graph of intensity against wavelength: a continuous curve rising from zero at a cut-off wavelength to a broad maximum and tailing off at long wavelengths, with two sharp characteristic peaks superimposed on it.]

The potential difference $V$ applied to the electrons incident on the metal is now increased.

Which of the following statements is correct?

A All the energy of the electrons is converted into X-rays.
B The wavelengths of the characteristic X-ray spectral lines are independent of the potential difference applied to accelerate the electrons.
C The maximum X-ray wavelength obtained is $\dfrac{hc}{eV}$.
D There is no change to the overall intensity of the X-ray spectrum.

stemImage.alt: Question 28: The diagram shows a sketch of the X-ray spectrum produced when electrons strike a metal target. The potential difference V applied to the electrons incident on

questions.difficultyReason: Needs knowledge of continuous vs characteristic X-ray features and the cut-off wavelength.
questions.misconception: Confusing the cut-off (minimum) wavelength with a maximum wavelength

explanation.body:
B is correct: the wavelengths of the characteristic X-ray lines depend on the material used to make the target, not on the potential difference applied to the electrons.

A is wrong: most of the electrons' energy goes towards heating the metal target. C is wrong: $\dfrac{hc}{eV}$ is the minimum wavelength. D is wrong: the intensity of the X-ray spectrum increases when $V$ is increased.

perOption.C: $hc/eV$ is the minimum (cut-off) wavelength, not the maximum.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A helium-neon laser emits red light having a wavelength of $6.4\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$ and a power of $0.5\ \mathrm{mW}$.

How many photons are emitted each second?

A $1.6\times10^{15}$
B $2.6\times10^{18}$
C $1.6\times10^{21}$
D $6.4\times10^{38}$

stemImage.alt: Question 27: A helium-neon laser emits red light having a wavelength of 6.4  10−7 m and a power of 0.5 mW. How many photons are emitted each second?

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation combines photon energy from wavelength with a milliwatt-to-watt conversion.
questions.misconception: Treating power as the energy of a single photon.

explanation.body: A photon has energy $hf$, so the emission rate is $N/t=P/(hf)=P\lambda/(hc)$. Substitution gives $(0.50\times10^{-3})(6.4\times10^{-7})/[(6.63\times10^{-34})(3.0\times10^8)]=1.6\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. It divides laser power by the energy per photon.
perOption.B: This rate would require about $0.81\ \mathrm{W}$ at the stated wavelength, indicating an error in the power scale.
perOption.C: Taking milli- as $10^3$ instead of $10^{-3}$ overstates the rate by a factor of $10^6$.
perOption.D: This rate implies a photon energy of about $7.8\times10^{-43}\ \mathrm{J}$, far below $hc/\lambda$.
